Alveolar tap [ɾ] plus close front [i]; from 照 'shining'

pronunciation.approximation: 'HOH-deh-ree' — the 'r' is a light tap, and all vowels are short and clear.
pronunciation.note: Hoderi is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is a minor but structurally important figure in the imperial genealogy.

domains.title: Fire-Shining Prince of the Sea
domains.subtitle: Fisherman, Elder Brother, and Tragic Heir
domains.lead: Hoderi is the elder son of the heavenly grandson Ninigi and the blossom princess Konohana-Sakuya-hime. His name means 'Fire-Shining,' and he was gifted with the fishhook that made him master of the sea. His story turns on the rivalry with his younger brother Hoori, a conflict that costs him his birthright and sets the imperial line on a new path.

cards.name: Master of the Sea
cards.desc: He received the fishhook and was meant to rule the waters.

cards.name: Elder Brother
cards.desc: Firstborn of Ninigi, but destined to lose precedence to Hoori.

cards.name: Tragic Competitor
cards.desc: His attempts to best Hoori end in the loss of his hook and his inheritance.

cards.name: Ancestral Figure
cards.desc: Ancestor of the Hayato, a people of southern Kyūshū.

symbols.name: Fishhook
symbols.meaning: The gift from Ninigi that gave him dominion over the sea

symbols.name: Fire
symbols.meaning: His name associates him with shining heat and the brilliance of the sun

symbols.name: Sea
symbols.meaning: The realm he was to master, contrasted with Hoori's mountains and fields

mythology.lead: Hoderi's story in the Kojiki is a tale of sibling rivalry, the exchange of gifts, and the transfer of sovereignty from the sea to the land.

myths.title: The Exchange of Gifts
myths.text: When Ninigi's sons grew up, he gave Hoderi the fishhook that ruled the sea and Hoori the bow that ruled the mountains. The brothers decided to exchange their gifts. Hoori, now with the hook, proved an inept fisherman and lost the hook in the sea. Hoderi demanded it back, and the quarrel drove Hoori into the undersea realm of the dragon god.

myths.title: Hoori's Triumph
myths.text: Hoori married Toyotama, the daughter of the sea god Ryūjin, and retrieved a magnificent hook. When he returned to land, the hook brought misfortune to Hoderi, reducing him to poverty and submission. Hoderi's descendants became the Hayato of southern Kyūshū, while Hoori's line produced the imperial ancestors.

myths.title: Ancestor of the Hayato
myths.text: The Kojiki traces the Hayato people — associated with Kyūshū and later with court ritual — back to Hoderi. Their role as ritual performers at the imperial court preserves the memory of the elder brother who was bypassed but not forgotten.

lore.syncretism: Hoderi is primarily a genealogical figure. He represents the sea and the older line that was superseded by the land-oriented imperial ancestry. His descendants, the Hayato, became part of the court's ritual apparatus, showing how myths of rivalry were transformed into structures of service.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hoderi is little known outside scholarly and ritual contexts, but his story underlies one of the key narratives of Japanese origins: the transfer of legitimacy from sea to land, from elder to younger, and the inclusion of older peoples within the imperial frame.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hoderi is the one who was passed over. His story asks us to notice the elder brother, the sea, the rival who does not win — and to see how myths of defeat are woven into national identity. Not every ancestor becomes emperor; some become memory.
lore.archaeology: Hoderi has no independent archaeological attestation. His importance is textual and genealogical, preserved in the Kojiki's account of the imperial lineage and in later references to the Hayato people.
